newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka industry hobbled by high rates.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka industry hobbled by high rates.

text.p: High interest rates caused by high inflation and large budget deficits are keeping Sri Lankan manufacturers from expanding, a top executive said on Thursday.

Kumar Dewapura, chairman of Tri-Star Apparel Exporters (Pte) Ltd, Sri Lanka's largest garment manufacturer, said his company had decided to seek a listing on the Colombo stock exchange next year to help slash its borrowing costs.
Economists said Sri Lankan interest rates were traditionally high due to inflation caused by high production costs, low productivity and large budget deficits.
They added that the 13-year-old civil war in the northeast had added to government expenditure.
Tri-Star, an associate of SR Gent Plc, also makes corrugated cartons, polybags and plastic coathangers for packing. Most of its output goes to Britain's Marks & Spencer Plc.
"The company will seek a listing on the Colombo Stock Exchange, mainly to reduce interest costs since equity is far cheaper than debt," Dewapura told Reuters.
Tri-Star was Sri Lanka's top corporate foreign exchange earner in 1995, bringing in 3.2 billion rupees ($58.18 million), according to Customs Department statisics.
"I can safely say that we passed the 1995 earnings in the first six months of 1996, and hope to end this year with almost double" that amount, Dewapura said. He gave no earnings figures.
Dewapura said Tri-Star, which has 27 factories and employs 24,600 people, needed a cheaper source of funds for expansion.

"We now have 12 outlets manufacturing exclusively for Marks & Spencer, up from eight at the end of 1995," he said, adding he hoped to open one more factory in the southern Matara area that would initially employ 500 workers.
"We can move even faster. But what is holding us back is high interes rates in the country," he said. "Tri-Star paid 160 million rupees in interest on rupee-loans in 1995."
Despite being a prime customer, commercial banks charge the company interest rates of 27 to 28 percent a month, he said.

"Even development banks lend at 23 to 24 percent," he said. A Central Bank official said that "high inflation results from high cost of production, low efficiency and high state spending," and that he saw no quick end to the problem.
Sri Lanka, which has seen double-digit inflation for most of the last decade, reported a year-on-year consumer price rise of 13.9 percent in August.
"The main problem in the country is the low productivity and efficiency you see everywhere," says Dewapura.
Dewapura criticised calls for a devaluation of the rupee by executives who say it will make their products more competitive overseas.
"That is an excuse made by industrialists who cannot, or do not want to, improve efficiency," he said.

Economists said any sharp devaluation of the rupee would fan inflation in Sri Lanka, which needed to import military hardware to fight the war and food to meet shortages caused by a severe drought this year.
Any "sharp devaluation will only serve to worsen the problem of high interest rates, which is largely due to inflation in the first place," said the central banker.
